rows.bounded_proposition: Specialist scholarship establishes slavery/nobi as a real and changing institution in medieval Korean history, while Tamna scholarship securely treats the Jeju island polity as a distinct historical target around the fifth–sixth centuries. The bounded review did not recover target-specific evidence sufficient to establish slavery, servile dependency, or another project coercion category in Tamna at the 500 CE anchor.
rows.required_abstention: Do not project peninsula-wide Korean slavery/nobi institutions onto Tamna; do not use later Goryeo/Joseon Jeju servitude, tribute, exile or Mongol-period institutions as evidence for 500 CE; do not infer absence from the target-specific evidentiary gap.
rows.temporal_applicability: Broader Korean slavery scholarship includes early medieval institutional development, but no positive Tamna-specific status evidence was recovered for the 500 CE anchor.
rows.temporal_precision: target identity overlaps fifth–sixth centuries; subject evidence remains broader Korean context rather than anchor-specific Tamna evidence
rows.evidence_locus: broader medieval Korean slavery scholarship plus target-specific Tamna historical studies; no decisive Tamna slavery/coercion locus recovered
rows.inference_extent: research coverage statement only; no Tamna territorial-practice inference
rows.law_practice_note: No Korean peninsula legal/status regime is silently assigned to autonomous island-polity Tamna.
rows.network_territorial_note: Tributary/diplomatic relations are not treated as territorial coercion evidence.
rows.language_access_limitations: English-accessible specialist slavery synthesis and Korean/English abstracts on ancient Tamna were reviewed. Korean-language Tamna-specific social-status and archaeological literature was not exhaustively reviewed, making the target-specific negative search materially access-limited.

sources.title: Slavery in Medieval Korea
sources.author: Seung B. Kye
sources.locator: Cambridge World History of Slavery vol.2, chapter 12, pp.295–312
sources.notes: Establishes the broader Korean slavery/nobi history but is not Tamna-specific; therefore it limits rather than licenses target inference.

sources.title: The Historical Understanding of Research and Major Issue of Tamna in Ancient

sources.author: Jang Chang-eun

sources.notes: Supports fifth–sixth-century Tamna naming/identity context only.

rows.bounded_proposition: Specialist synthesis securely documents slavery and hereditary/unfree dependency in medieval Tamil South India, including a substantial rise in thirteenth-century inscriptional references, temple purchases and gifts of people described as atimai, and clearly unfree monastery slaves. The same synthesis warns that virtually all surviving twelfth–thirteenth-century slave inscriptions are concentrated in present-day Thanjavur district. The bounded packet therefore establishes a strong contemporary Tamil-country slavery context but does not safely synchronize the decisive inscriptional loci with the Pandya Empire frame at exactly 1300 CE.
rows.required_abstention: Do not equate 'Tamil country' with the Pandya polity, silently assign Thanjavur slave inscriptions to Pandya rule without source-level political synchronization, treat devotional atiyar language as literal slavery, or infer empire-wide prevalence from temple-centered inscription survival.
rows.temporal_applicability: The decisive slavery evidence is twelfth–thirteenth century and therefore near/overlapping the 1300 anchor, but political/spatial applicability to the frozen Pandya polity has not been established tightly enough for a positive selected-year territorial claim.
rows.temporal_precision: thirteenth-century and early-fourteenth-century regional inscriptional synthesis; exact target-polity synchronization unresolved
rows.evidence_locus: medieval Tamil-country temple and monastery inscriptions, especially Thanjavur district; not yet securely bounded to the Pandya Empire at 1300
rows.inference_extent: contemporary regional slavery/dependency context only; no Pandya-wide or selected-year territorial-practice classification
rows.law_practice_note: Temple sale/gift records support bounded statuses and transactions; they do not establish a single empire-wide legal regime.
rows.language_access_limitations: English-language specialist synthesis grounded in Tamil inscriptions was reviewed. The underlying Tamil epigraphic corpus was not exhaustively re-read inscription by inscription for contemporaneous Pandya jurisdiction, and that unresolved spatial synchronization is decisive.

sources.title: Slavery and Dependency in Medieval South India
sources.author: Leslie C. Orr
sources.locator: Cambridge World History of Slavery vol.2, ch.13, pp.313–334; esp. pp.320–327 on atimai, thirteenth-century slave references and their Thanjavur concentration
sources.notes: Strong evidence for medieval Tamil slavery/dependency; its own spatial/source-survival discussion blocks automatic conversion into a Pandya-1300 territorial claim.

sources.title: Donors, Devotees, and Daughters of God: Temple Women in Medieval Tamilnadu
sources.author: Leslie C. Orr
sources.locator: terminological discussion of atiyar/atimai and temple women; notes around pp.52–57 and 216
sources.notes: Clarifies that atimai is the clearer inscriptional slavery term while related devotional terminology can be ambiguous; materially overlaps Orr's later synthesis.

rows.bounded_proposition: Archaeological scholarship on the Chimú polity describes a political economy characterized by state control over land, water and labor resources and, in conquered/administrative territories, tribute and labor service directed toward the capital. Specialist work places a major phase of Chimú expansion at about 1300 and identifies administrative oversight of canal construction and corvée labor. This supports a bounded classification of state labor-service/corvée coercion within the Chimú system at the 1300 anchor.
rows.required_abstention: Do not relabel Chimú labor service as chattel slavery, infer permanent personal unfreedom, assume every household or province was subject to identical coercion, or treat debated forced-resettlement models at Cerro la Virgen as established empire-wide fact.
rows.temporal_applicability: Specialist archaeological syntheses place Chimú state organization across AD 1000–1476 and a major expansion phase beginning about 1300; the reviewed labor-administration evidence spans the anchor.
rows.temporal_precision: archaeological phase/range evidence rather than an exact annual event
rows.evidence_locus: Chimú heartland and administrative/provincial systems on the north coast of Peru, including Moche/Chan Chan and conquered valleys
rows.inference_extent: bounded state labor service/corvée and extraction; not slavery status, uniform household coercion, or an empire-wide intensity score
rows.law_practice_note: The claim is archaeological/political-economic practice, not a reconstructed formal legal code.
rows.language_access_limitations: English-language archaeological scholarship and source summaries reviewed. The evidence is primarily material/archaeological and partly model-based; colonial ethnohistoric analogies are treated as supporting context rather than sole proof.

sources.title: Imperialist Expansion in Peruvian Prehistory: Chimu Administration of a Conquered Territory
sources.author: Richard W. Keatinge; Geoffrey W. Conrad
sources.locator: Journal of Field Archaeology 10(3), pp.255–283; abstract/model of state control and tribute/labor service
sources.notes: Directly models Chimú state control of labor resources and extractive tribute/labor service; supports coercive labor-service category, not slavery.

sources.title: Chimu Administration in the Provinces
sources.author: Carol J. Mackey
sources.locator: The Origins and Development of the Andean State, pp.121–129; eHRAF publication metadata/abstract
sources.notes: Places a new expansion phase about AD 1300 and describes administrative functions including canal construction and corvée labor; also stresses variable political control across conquered territory.

sources.title: Fisherman, Farmer, Rich Man, Poor Man, Weaver, Parcialidad Chief? Household Archaeology at Cerro la Virgen, a Chimú Town within the Hinterland of Chan Chan
sources.author: Brian R. Billman; Dana Bardolph; Jean Hudson; Jesús Briceño Rosario
sources.locator: Maritime Communities of the Ancient Andes, ch.10, pp.267–300; discussion/conclusion on labor-tax models and household autonomy
sources.notes: Tests older forced-labor-colony interpretations and finds no local evidence for forced labor at Cerro la Virgen, supporting a bounded rather than uniform empire-wide claim.
